# Neonatal MIS-C

**Authors:** Priyam Pattnaik, Manan Shah, Greshma Susan George

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

The World Health Organization (WHO) declared a coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic in March 2020. Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) causes COVID-19 infection, which may present with acute respiratory distress syndrome, affecting individuals of all ages. In adults, COVID-19 commonly leads to acute respiratory failure. In children, COVID-19 usually has a milder clinical course and a more favorable outcome. In contrast to adults and older children, COVID-19 infection is uncommon in neonates.  The low incidence of COVID-19 infection in neonates is attributed to the limited availability of angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors in the nasal epithelium, considered the primary point of entry for COVID-19 in the human body. However, hyperinflammatory shock and organ failure cases were reported in neonates and older children with previous COVID-19 infection and positive antibodies. Subsequently, a different disease entity associated with COVID-19 in children was described as a multisystem inflammatory syndrome related to COVID-19 (MIS-C). The definition of MIS-C related to COVID-19 has undergone significant changes. The original Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) definition posed challenges in differentiating MIS-C from severe COVID-19, prompting revisions by the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) and the CDC. Implemented on January 1, 2023, the new criteria include notable modifications, such as removing the requirement for fever duration; the requirement of involvement of at least two organ systems, with shock added as a separate category; and specification of elevated C-reactive protein (CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL) as an inflammatory marker. The timeframe for MIS-C diagnosis was extended to up to 60 days following a positive SARS-CoV-2 test result. These revisions improve the distinction between MIS-C and other illnesses, reduce misclassification, and enhance the feasibility of implementation. The updated definition eliminates respiratory, neurologic, and renal criteria and designates Kawasaki disease as an alternative diagnosis. See Image. Surveillance Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children.
